greek: κᾂν μὲν τοῦθ’ οὕτως ἔχῃ, θαυμαστὸν οὐδὲν, εἰ μὴ μόνον τοῖς ληθαργικοῖς, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς φρενιτικοῖς [655] συμπίπτῃ. τὸ δ’ οὐχ ὑπνῶδες κῶμα τούτοις μὲν οὐκ ἔστιν ἴδιον, γίνεται δ’ ἐνίοτε. εὑρήσεις γὰρ πολλοὺς φρενιτικοὺς οὔτε ἀνισταμένους οὔτε ἐπαίρειν τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ὅλως δυναμένους, ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ μένοντας ὁμοίους τοῖς ληθαργικοῖς, ὥστε τούτους οἱ πολλοὶ καὶ ἀπαίδευτοι τῶν ἰατρῶν, οὔτε τί δεῖ καλεῖν οἴδασιν, ἀλλὰ παντάπασιν ἀποροῦσι, καὶ ἀλλότριον δοκεῖ αὐτοῖς εἶναι τοῦτο τὸ πάθος καὶ ἀνώνυμον, ἔνιοι δὲ σύμμικτόν ἐκ ληθάργου τε καὶ φρενίτιδος ὑπολαμβάνουσι, καὶ προσαγορεύουσι τυφομανίαν. καὶ τὸ κάκιστον πάντων, τινὲς τῶν Ἱπποκρατείων εἶναι προσποιουμένων τοῦτό φασι, καίτοι δήπου σαφῶς οὕτω καὶ φανερῶς γράφοντος Ἱπποκράτους, οὐκ ἐν ἀμφιδόξῳ βιβλίῳ, ἀλλ’ εἴπερ τις ἄλλος τῶν γνησίων εἶναι πεπιστευμένῳ τῷ τρίτῳ τῶν ἐπιδημιῶν, οὔτ’ ἐξεμάνη τῶν φρενιτικῶν οὐδεὶς, ὥσπερ ἐπ’ ἄλλοισιν, ἀλλ’ ἄλλῃ τινὶ καταφορῇ νωθρῇ βαρέως ἀπώλλυντο. οὐ μόνον γὰρ ὅτι καταφορὰ ταῖς φρενίτισιν ἐνίοτε συμπίπτει διήγγειλεν, ἀλλ’ ὅτι καὶ νωθρὰ πολλάκις. τίς δ’ ἡ νωθρά;
rendering_1: And if this is so, it is nothing remarkable if it befalls not only lethargics but also phrenitics. [655] The non-somnolent coma, however, is not peculiar to these latter, but it does occur at times. For you will find many phrenitics who neither get up nor are able to raise their eyes at all, but remain in the same position like lethargics, so that the common run of uneducated physicians do not know what these ought to be called, but are altogether at a loss, and this affection seems to them to be something foreign and nameless, while some suppose it to be a mixture compounded of lethargy and phrenitis, and name it typhomania. And, worst of all, some of those who pretend to be Hippocrateans say this, although Hippocrates surely writes so clearly and manifestly, not in a book of disputed authenticity but in one which, if any other, is believed to be among the genuine works, the third book of the Epidemics: "nor did any of the phrenitics go raving mad, as in other cases, but they perished heavily with some other sluggish sinking (kataphora)." For he announced not only that sinking sometimes befalls cases of phrenitis, but also that it is often sluggish. And what is the sluggish one?
rendering_2: And if this is so, it is no wonder if [coma] befalls not only lethargic patients but also phrenitic [655] patients. The coma that is not sleepy, however, is not proper to the latter, though it does occur sometimes. For you will find many phrenitics who neither get up nor are able to raise their eyes at all, but remain in the same position, like lethargic patients. So the majority of physicians, the uneducated ones, do not know what they ought to call these patients; they are entirely at a loss, and this affection seems to them foreign and nameless. Some suppose it to be a mixture of lethargy and phrenitis, and call it typhomania. And worst of all, some of those who profess to be Hippocrateans say this, although surely Hippocrates writes thus clearly and plainly, not in a book of disputed authenticity but in the third book of the Epidemics, which is believed, if any other is, to be among the genuine ones: 'nor did any of the phrenitics go raving mad, as in other cases, but they perished grievously in some other sluggish torpor.' For he reported not only that torpor sometimes befalls cases of phrenitis, but also that it is often sluggish. And what is the sluggish one?

greek: παραπλήσιον γάρ τι συμβαίνει πολλῶν ἀρχομένοις νοσημάτων, οἷον ἔν τισι [664] τῶν μεθυσθέντων ἔστιν ἰδεῖν γιγνόμενον. ὅταν μὲν κωματώδεις ὦσι, καὶ σφάλλονται, καὶ βαρῶσι τὴν κεφαλὴν, καὶ μηδ’ εἰ βιάζοιντο διαίρειν δύνανται τὰ βλέφαρα· δι’ αὐτὸ δ’ αὖ πάλιν τοῦτο τὸ βάρος ὑπνοῦν ἀδυνατοῦσιν ἀσώμενοι, καὶ στρεφόμενοι, καὶ ῥιπτοῦντες ἑαυτοὺς, καὶ μεταβάλλοντες ἄλλοτ’ εἰς ἄλλο σχῆμα. ταῦτα γὰρ ἔστιν ἰδεῖν πολλάκις ἐπὶ τῶν μεθυσθέντων γιγνόμενα, πληρωθείσης αὐτῶν ἐν τῇ μέθῃ τῆς κεφαλῆς, εἶθ’ ὑπὸ τοῦ βάρους ἅμα τ’ εἰς κῶμα κατασπώσης ἅμα τε ὕπνον κωλυούσης. οὕτως οὖν καὶ πλήθους ἀπέπτου τὴν κεφαλὴν κατειληφότος, ἄγρυπνοί τε ἅμα καὶ κωματώδεις εἰσίν. καὶ τοῦτο κατ’ ἀρχὰς γενόμενον, ἔστιν ὅτε μὲν πεφθῇ καλῶς, ὥσπερ καὶ ἐξ οἴνου τοιοῦτο εἴη γεγονός· ἀλλ’ οὕτω μὲν οὔτε λήθαργος, οὔτε φρενῖτις ἠκολούθησεν· ἔστιν ὅτε δὲ δριμὺ γενόμενον εἰς φρενίτιδα ἐτελεύτησε. πολλοῖς δ’ αὖ τὸ μὲν λεπτότερον ἢ πεφθὲν ἢ διαφορηθὲν ἐκενώθη, ὑπέμεινε δὲ τὸ παχύτερον, καὶ οὕτω λήθαργος ἐπεγένετο.
rendering_1: For something similar happens to those at the beginning of many diseases, such as one can see occurring in some [664] of those who have become drunk. When they are comatose, they both stagger and are heavy in the head, and are unable to part their eyelids even if they were to force themselves; yet, on the other hand, through this very heaviness they are unable to sleep, being in distress, turning about, throwing themselves around, and changing now to one posture, now to another. For one can often see these things occurring in those who have become drunk, when their head has been filled during the drunkenness and then, by its heaviness, at the same time drags them down into coma and prevents sleep. So also, then, when an unconcocted plethora has taken hold of the head, they are at once sleepless and comatose. And when this arises at the beginning, sometimes it is concocted well, just as would also be the case if such a condition had arisen from wine; but in this case neither lethargus nor phrenitis followed. Sometimes, however, having become acrid, it ended in phrenitis. In many, again, the thinner part, having been either concocted or dispersed, was evacuated, while the thicker part remained, and in this way lethargus supervened.
rendering_2: For something similar happens to people at the beginning of many diseases, such as one may see occurring in some [664] of those who have become drunk. When they are comatose, they both stagger and are heavy in the head, and cannot raise their eyelids even if they force themselves; yet on account of this very heaviness, in turn, they are unable to sleep, being in distress, tossing about, throwing themselves this way and that, and changing now into one posture, now into another. For these things can often be seen occurring in those who have become drunk, their head having been filled in the drunkenness and then, by its heaviness, at once dragging them down into coma and at once preventing sleep. So too, then, when an unconcocted plenitude has taken hold of the head, they are at the same time both sleepless and comatose. And when this occurs at the beginning, sometimes it is well concocted, just as such a thing would have come about from wine as well; but in that case neither lethargy nor phrenitis followed; sometimes, however, it became acrid and ended in phrenitis. In many, again, the thinner part was evacuated, either by being concocted or by being dispersed, while the thicker part remained, and thus lethargy supervened.

greek: προεληλυθότος μὲν τοῦ τοιούτου νοσήματος, ἡ τοιαύτη διάθεσις, ὡς μὲν ἡμεῖς ἐδείξαμεν, ἐγγὺς ἤδη φρενίτιδος· ὡς δ’ οἱ τὸ μικτὸν πάθος ἐκ ληθάργου [665] καὶ φρενίτιδος εἰσάγοντες ὑπολαμβάνουσιν, ἐκείνῳ δόξειεν ἂν εἶναι συγγενεστέρα. πότερον δ’ ἤδη τοὺς οὕτως ἔχοντας ὀνομάζειν χρὴ φρενιτικοὺς, ἢ ὀλίγου ὕστερον ἔσεσθαι προσδοκᾷν, τοῦθ’ ἑτέρας ἂν εἴη σκέψεως, οὔτ’ ὠφελούσης τι τὰ νῦν προκείμενα, καὶ ἄλλως διὰ τοῦ εἰσίν, ὃ καί τινες προσγράφουσι τῷ ἆρα φρενιτικοὶ, τινὲς δ’ οὔ.
rendering_1: When such a disease has advanced, such a condition is, as we have shown, already close to phrenitis; but as those who introduce the mixed affection compounded of lethargus [665] and phrenitis suppose, it would seem to be more akin to that. Whether one ought already to call those so disposed phrenitics, or to expect that they will become so a little later, this would belong to another inquiry, one that contributes nothing to the matters now before us, and that besides turns on the word 'are' (εἰσίν), which some add to 'are they then phrenitics' (ἆρα φρενιτικοί), while others do not.
rendering_2: When such a disease has progressed, this kind of condition, as we have shown, is already close to phrenitis; but as those who introduce the mixed affection compounded of lethargy [665] and phrenitis suppose, it would seem to be more akin to that. Whether, however, one should already call those in such a state phrenitics, or should expect that they will be so a little later, this would belong to another inquiry, one that neither contributes anything to what is now before us, and in any case (turns) on the word 'are' (εἰσίν), which some also add to the 'ἆρα φρενιτικοί' and others do not.

greek: μεμνήσῃ πρῶτον μὲν τῆς διαιρέσεως, ἂν μὴ μέλλῃς τὰ παρόντα [656] παρακούειν, ὅταν καταφορὰν τὴν μὲν ὑπνώδη, τὴν δὲ ἄγρυπνον ἐκάλουν, καὶ τὴν μὲν ὑπνώδη ἰδίαν εἶναι τῶν ληθαργικῶν καὶ διαπαντὸς ὑπάρχειν αὐτοῖς, τὴν δὲ οὔτε ἰδίαν εἶναι τῶν φρενιτικῶν οὔτε ὑπάρχειν αὐτοῖς διαπαντός. Ἡ μὲν οὖν ὑπνώδης, ὅσον ἐπὶ τῷ παρόντι, τοῖς ληθαργικοῖς συμπίπτει· τὴν δ’ ἄγρυπνον, ἥτις τοῖς φρενιτικοῖς ἐπιγίγνεται, πειράσομαι διορίζειν, ἵνα δυνηθῇς εὑρίσκειν τὴν ὑφ’ Ἱπποκράτους εἰρημένην διαφοράν. οὐ γὰρ ἦν τῶν ματαίως τὰ ὀνόματα ἐπιτιθέντων οὗτος ὁ ἀνὴρ, οὔτ’ ἀνοήτως πρόσκειται τῇ καταφορᾷ τὸ νωθρὰ, οὔτε φησιν, ὥσπερ Ὅμηρος, ὑγρὸν ἔλαιον καὶ γάλα λευκὸν, μηδενὸς ἕνεκα διορισμοῦ· καὶ γὰρ πᾶν γάλα λευκὸν καὶ ἔλαιον ὑγρόν· ἀλλ’ ἑκάστη λέξις καὶ συλλαβὴ πᾶσα πρᾶγμά τι σημαίνει παρ’ αὐτοῦ.
rendering_1: You will remember, first of all, the division—if you are not going to misunderstand what is presently [656] being said—when I called one kind of catophora sleepy and the other sleepless, and (said) that the sleepy kind is proper to lethargics and is present in them throughout, whereas the other is neither proper to phrenitics nor present in them throughout. The sleepy kind, then, so far as concerns the present matter, befalls lethargics; the sleepless kind, which supervenes in phrenitics, I shall try to delimit, so that you may be able to discover the difference spoken of by Hippocrates. For this man was not one of those who apply names at random, nor is the word 'sluggish' added to catophora thoughtlessly, nor does he say, as Homer does, 'liquid oil' and 'white milk' for the sake of no distinction at all—for indeed all milk is white and all oil liquid—but with him every word and every syllable signifies some real thing.
rendering_2: You will remember, first, the division, if you are not going to mishear what is now being said [656]: I called one kind of kataphora sleepy and the other wakeful, and said that the sleepy kind is proper to lethargics and always present in them, while the other is neither proper to phrenitics nor always present in them. The sleepy kind, then, as far as the present matter goes, occurs in lethargics. The wakeful kind, which supervenes in phrenitics, I shall try to define, so that you may be able to find the difference stated by Hippocrates. For this man was not one of those who apply names idly. The word 'torpid' is not attached to 'kataphora' senselessly, nor does he say, as Homer does, 'liquid oil' and 'white milk' for the sake of no distinction at all, for all milk is white and all oil liquid. With him, rather, every word and every syllable signifies some thing.

greek: ἐν πάσαις γὰρ ταῖς εἰρημέναις ῥήσεσιν [645] ἀγρυπνίας καὶ κώματος φαίνεται μνημονεύων. ἕτερον δ’ ἄῤῥωστον αὖθις γράφων ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ βιβλίῳ φησί· τουτέῳ διὰ τέλεος, ἐξ οὗ καὶ ἐγὼ οἶδα, κοιλίη ταραχώδης, οὖρα λεπτὰ μέλανα, κωματώδης, ἄγρυπνος. ὥστ’ ἄντικρυς εἶναι δῆλον, ὅτι μηδ’ ὕπνον, μηδὲ καταφορὰν παρ’ αὐτῷ δηλοῖ τὸ τοῦ κώματος ὄνομα. διὰ τοῦτο, οἶμαι, τινὲς τῶν ἐξηγητῶν ἀπὸ τοῦ κωμάζειν φασὶ τοὺς κωματώδεις ὠνομάσθαι· ἐγρηγορέναι μὲν γὰρ καὶ τοὺς κωμάζοντας, ἐγρηγορέναι δὲ καὶ τοὺς κωματώδεις. καὶ νὴ Δία ὥσπερ οἱ κωμάζοντες οὐ πάνυ τι κατανεύουσιν, οὕτως οὐδὲ τοὺς κωματίζοντας, καὶ μάλιστα τοῖν ὀφθαλμοῖν. ὑγρούς τε γὰρ εἶναι καὶ ἐρυθροὺς καὶ ἀστηρίκτους καὶ ἐνδεδυμένους· ἀλλὰ τὸ πᾶν ἀμφοτέροις σῶμα σφαλερὸν ἐν ταῖς κινήσεσι καὶ ἀκρατές· αὐτὸν διὰ τοῦτο καὶ τὸν Ἱπποκράτην περὶ τῆς ὅλης συνδρομῆς ἀπορεῖν, εἴτε χρὴ φρενιτικοὺς αὐτοὺς ὀνομάζειν, εἴτ’ ἄλλο τι.
rendering_1: For in all the passages cited [645] he is evidently making mention of sleeplessness and coma. And again, writing of another patient in the same book, he says: "In this man throughout, from the time when I too had knowledge of him, the bowels were disturbed, urine thin and black; comatose, sleepless." So that it is plainly evident that in him the name of coma signifies neither sleep nor kataphora. For this reason, I think, some of the commentators say that the comatose are named from revelling (kōmazein); for those who revel are awake, and the comatose are awake as well. And, by Zeus, just as revellers do not altogether nod downward, so neither do those in a state of coma (κωματίζοντας), and especially as regards the two eyes: for these are moist and red and unsteady and sunken (ἐνδεδυμένους); but the whole body in both is unsteady in its movements and without control; and that for this reason Hippocrates himself is at a loss concerning the whole concurrence of symptoms, whether one ought to call them phrenitic or something else.
rendering_2: For in all the passages quoted he evidently mentions [645] both sleeplessness and coma. And again, writing of another patient in the same book, he says: 'In this man throughout, from the time that I too knew him, the bowel was disturbed, urine thin, black; he was comatose, sleepless.' So it is plainly evident that with him the name of coma signifies neither sleep nor torpor (kataphora). For this reason, I suppose, some of the exegetes say that the comatose are named from 'revelling' (kōmazein). For revellers are awake, and the comatose are awake too. And, by Zeus, just as revellers do not nod down at all, so neither do those in a coma, and especially not with their eyes. For their eyes are moist and red and unsteady and sunken. But in both the whole body is unsteady in its movements and lacking in control. For this reason, they say, Hippocrates himself is also at a loss about the whole syndrome, whether one should call these patients phrenitics or something else.

greek: καὶ πάλιν, ἐν ﻿ [663] ἀφωνίῃ πνεῦμα, οἷον τοῖσι πνιγομένοισι πρόχειρον, πονηρόν. ἆρά γε καὶ παρακρουστικὸν τὸ τοιοῦτον; εἰ τοίνυν χρὴ κεφαλὴν ἐπιδοῦναι τῷ λόγῳ, καὶ μήτ’ ἄλλος τις τῶν Ἑλλήνων οὕτω κέχρηται τῷ ἆρα συνδέσμῳ μήθ’ Ἱπποκράτης αὐτὸς, ὡς ἐγὼ νῦν ἔδειξα, μέμψαιτ’ ἄν τις, οἶμαι, τοὺς ἐξηγησαμένους ὡς οὐκ ἀπορητικὸν σύνδεσμον. Καί τοι χαλεπώτερον ἐμαυτὸν τὸν λόγον ἐπίσταμαι ποιεῖν. διωρισμένης γὰρ τῆς ὑπνώδους καταφορᾶς ἀπὸ τῆς οὐχ ὑπνώδους φρενίτιδος, οὐκ ἂν ἔτι δεόντως ἀπορῶν φαίνοιτο καὶ μὴ βεβαίως ἀποφαινόμενος φρενιτικοὺς εἶναι τοὺς τοιούτους. ἀλλ’ ἧττον γὰρ ἐμοὶ μέλει τῆς ἐν τοῖς λόγοις χαλεπότητος ἢ τῆς ἀληθείας, ὅτι τε ἀπορητικός ἐστιν ὁ σύνδεσμος, ὁμολογῶ, καὶ δείξω τὴν αἰτίαν, δι’ ἣν οὐκ ἐτόλμησε φρενιτικοὺς εἶναι τοὺς τοιούτους ἀποφήνασθαι ὁ Ἱπποκράτης, ἀλλ’ ἔτ’ ἀπορεῖ. τὸ γὰρ ἐν ἀρχῇσι προσκείμενον τὴν πάσαν ἔχει τοῦ λόγου δύναμιν, ὃ παραλείπουσιν οἱ πολλοὶ τῶν ἐξηγητῶν, ὥσπερ μάτην προσγεγραμμένον.
rendering_1: And again: "In aphonia, breathing that is hurried, as in those who are being choked, is bad. Is such a thing also deranging?" If, then, one must put a head on the argument: since neither any other of the Greeks has used the conjunction ἆρα in this way, nor Hippocrates himself, as I have now shown, one would, I think, find fault with those who have expounded it as not an aporetic conjunction. And yet I know that I am making the argument harder for myself. For since the somnolent kataphora has been distinguished from phrenitis, which is not somnolent, he would no longer appear to be properly in doubt and not firmly declaring such patients to be phrenitic. But since I care less about the difficulty in arguments than about the truth, I both concede that the conjunction is aporetic, and I shall show the reason on account of which Hippocrates did not dare to declare such patients phrenitic but is still in doubt. For the phrase added, "at the beginnings", holds the whole force of the statement, and most of the exegetes pass over it, as though it had been written in to no purpose.
rendering_2: And again: "in [663] aphonia, breathing such as in those being suffocated, shallow, is bad. Is such a thing also a sign of delirium?" If, then, one must put a head on the argument: since neither any other of the Greeks has used the conjunction ἆρα in that way, nor Hippocrates himself, as I have now shown, one would, I think, find fault with those who have interpreted it as not being a dubitative conjunction. And yet I am aware that I am making the argument more difficult for myself. For once the somnolent cataphora has been distinguished from the non-somnolent phrenitis, he would no longer appear to be properly at a loss and to be refraining from declaring firmly that such persons are phrenitic. But since I care less about difficulty in arguments than about the truth, I both admit that the conjunction is dubitative, and I shall show the cause on account of which Hippocrates did not venture to declare such persons to be phrenitic, but is still in doubt. For the added phrase "at the beginnings" holds the whole force of the statement—a phrase which most of the commentators pass over, as though it had been written in to no purpose.

greek: ἐπάρματα δὲ παρὰ τὰ ὦτα πολλοῖσιν ἑτερόῤῥοπα ἦν, καὶ ἐξ ἀμφοτέρων τοῖσι πλείστοισιν, ἀπύροισιν ὀρθοστάδην, ἔστι δ’ οἷς καὶ [652] σμικρὰ ἐπεθερμαίνοντο, κατέσβη πᾶσιν ἀσινέως, οὐδ’ ἐξεπύησεν οὐδενὶ, ὥσπερ τὰ ἐξ ἄλλων προφάσεων. ὄντως γὰρ παράλογον, μηδὲν ἐκπυῆσαι, καὶ οὐκ εἰθισμένα πάντως. εἶτ’ ἐπιφέρει, ἦν δ’ ὁ τρόπος αὐτέων, χαῦνα, μεγάλα, κεχυμένα, οὐ μετὰ φλεγμονῆς· παράλογον γὰρ χωρὶς φλεγμονῆς ἅπασι γενέσθαι τὰς περὶ τὰ ὦτα ἀποστάσεις. ὥστε φέρειν πάλιν κᾀνταῦθα τὸ κῶμα φαίνεται ἐπὶ καταφορᾶς τῆς ὑπνώδους, ὅταν λέγῃ· ἦν δὲ τὸ κῶμα συνεχὲς, οὐχ ὑπνῶδες· ὡς γὰρ ὑπνῶδες εἶναι δέον αὐτὸ, καὶ ὡς τοιοῦτο ἀεὶ γιγνόμενον, εἶτα νῦν παραλόγως οὐ γιγνόμενον, ἐπισημαίνεται. τὸ δ’, ὅταν ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ βιβλίῳ τῷ τρίτῳ τῶν ἐπιδημιῶν ἐπὶ τοῦ Πυθίωνος εἴπῃ, ἐννάτῃ κωματώδης, ἀσώδης, ὅτε διεγείροιτο· σαφῶς γὰρ κᾀνταῦθα τὸ κῶμα καταφοράν τινα δηλοῦν ἔοικεν. ἀλλ’ οὐχ οἷόν τέ φασιν ἅμα καταφέρεσθαι καὶ ἀγρυπνεῖν. ταῦτα γὰρ οἱ θαυμαστοὶ λέγουσιν ἐξηγηταὶ, μὴ γιγνώσκοντες, ὅτι δύο εἰσὶν εἴδη καταφορᾶς, ὡς οἵ τε δοκιμώτατοι τῶν ἰατρῶν γεγράφασι καὶ αὐτὰ τὰ γιγνόμενα μαρτυρεῖ.
rendering_1: "Swellings beside the ears occurred in many on one side, and on both sides in most, in persons without fever and going about upright; in some, however, they also [652] became slightly heated; they subsided in all without harm, and did not suppurate in any, as do those arising from other causes." For it is truly contrary to expectation that none should suppurate, and altogether not what is customary. Then he adds: "their character was loose, large, diffuse, without inflammation"; for it is contrary to expectation that the abscessions about the ears should arise in all without inflammation. So that here too again he appears to apply "coma" to the sleepy kataphora, when he says: "the coma was continuous, not sleepy"; for he notes it as though it ought to be sleepy, and as always occurring in that form, but now, contrary to expectation, not occurring so. And as for when, in the same book, the third of the Epidemics, in the case of Pythion, he says, "on the ninth day comatose, nauseated when he was roused"—for here too "coma" clearly seems to indicate a certain kataphora. But, they say, it is not possible to be borne down in kataphora and to be sleepless at the same time. For this is what the admirable commentators say, not knowing that there are two kinds of kataphora, as both the most approved of the physicians have written and the very facts themselves bear witness.

Then he adds: 'Their character was lax, large, diffuse, not with inflammation'; for it is contrary to expectation that in all of them the abscessions about the ears should occur without inflammation. So here too he plainly applies the term coma to the somnolent kataphora, when he says: 'The coma was continuous, not somnolent.' He remarks on this as if it ought to be somnolent and always became so, and now, contrary to expectation, did not. And what of the passage in the same book, the third of the Epidemics, where he says of Pythion: 'On the ninth day, comatose, nauseous whenever he was roused'? For here too coma clearly seems to indicate a kind of kataphora. 'But,' they say, 'it is not possible to be in kataphora and to be sleepless at the same time.' This is what these admirable exegetes say, not knowing that there are two kinds of kataphora, as both the most esteemed of the physicians have written and the phenomena themselves attest.

greek: φέρε εἰπεῖν, ὅπως τὸ λεγόμενον σαφὲς γένηται καὶ τοῖς ἧττον [661] γεγυμνασμένοις, τὸ ἆρά γε ἡμέρα ἐστί; καὶ, ἆρά γε ἐλεύσεται σήμερον; ἀπορητικὸν ἔχει ἐπίῤῥημα. ἂν δὲ λόγῳ ἀποφαίνειν αὐτοῖς βουληθῶ, ἤτοι ἁπλῶς λέγων οὕτω χωρὶς πάσης ἀποδείξεως, ἐλεύσεται σήμερον· ἤτοι μετ’ ἀποδείξεως οὕτως, ἐὰν ἥλιος ὑπὲρ γῆν ἐστιν, ἡμέρα ἐστίν· ἐὰν περιπατεῖ, κινεῖται ἄρα. ὅταν δὲ χωρὶς ἀποδείξεως ἀποφαίνωμέν τι, οὐ δεόμεθα τοῦ ἄρα ἐπιῤῥήματος, περιττὸς γάρ ἐστιν ὁ λόγος, καὶ οὐδεὶς οὕτω φησὶν, ἡμέρα ἐστὶν ἄρα, οὔθ’ οὕτως, ἀρά γε ἡμέρα ἐστὶν, ἐπειδὰν ἐξῇ λέγειν οὕτως ἁπλῶς, ἡμέρα ἐστίν. οὔθ’ οὕτω κατ’ ἀπόδειξιν οἷόν τέ ἐστι χρῆσθαι αὐτὸν τῷ ἆρά γε. πῶς γὰρ ἂν εἴη ἀπόδειξις, πάσης ἀποδείξεως ἐξ ἑτέρων λημμάτων ἕτερον λῆμμα καταλαμβανούσης; ἀλλὰ μηδὲν φαίνεται νῦν λῆμμα συλλογιστικὸν εἰς ἀπόδειξιν λαμβάνων. πῶς οὖν τὸ ἆρά γε ἐπίῤῥημα γενήσεται ἀντ’ ἀπορητικοῦ συλλογιστικὸν καὶ συμπεραντικόν;
rendering_1: Let me say, so that what is being said may become clear also to those less [661] trained: the 'ἆρά γε, is it day?' and 'ἆρά γε, will he come today?' contain a dubitative adverb. But if I wish to make a declaration to them in speech, I do so either by simply saying thus, without any demonstration, 'he will come today', or with demonstration, thus: 'if the sun is above the earth, it is day'; 'if he walks, therefore (ἄρα) he moves'. Now when we declare something without demonstration, we have no need of the adverb ἄρα, for the expression is superfluous, and no one says thus, 'it is day, therefore (ἄρα)', nor thus, 'ἆρά γε, it is day', when it is possible to say simply thus, 'it is day'. Nor is it possible that he uses ἆρά γε in that way, by way of demonstration. For how could there be a demonstration, when every demonstration establishes one premise out of other premises? But he is evidently not now taking any syllogistic premise for a demonstration. How then will the adverb ἆρά γε become, instead of dubitative, syllogistic and conclusive?

greek: ἑτέρου [644] πράγματος ἐκεῖνοι τοὔνομα φέρουσιν, οὐδὲν κωλύει τὸν Ἱπποκράτην διαφερόντως χρῆσθαι. αὐτίκα παρὰ τῷ ποιητῇ δόξειεν ἂν ὕπνον δηλοῦν τοὔνομα· Ἦ με μάλ’ αἰνοπαθῆ μαλακὸν περὶ κῶμ’ ἐκάλυψεν. καὶ — — ἐπεὶ αὐτῷ ἐγὼ μαλακὸν περὶ κῶμα κάλυψα. ἀλλ’ οὐχ Ἱπποκράτης οὕτω φαίνεται χρώμενος, εἴγε καὶ μετὰ ἀγρυπνίας πολλάκις τὸ κῶμα γίγνεσθαί φησι καὶ φρενιτικοῖς συνεδρεύειν. ἐν ἀρχῇ μὲν τοῦ προῤῥητικοῦ τάδε γράφει· οἱ κωματώδεες ἐν ἀρχῇσι γινόμενοι, μετὰ κεφαλῆς, ὀσφύος, ὑποχονδρίου, τραχήλου ὀδύνης, ἀγρυπνέοντες, ἆρά γε φρενιτικοί εἰσιν; ἐν δὲ τῷ τρίτῳ τῶν ἐπιδημιῶν (ἀπό τινων τῶν ὁμολογουμένων αὐτοῦ γνησίων βιβλίων λάβωμεν τὰς μαρτυρίας) ὧδέ πως φησιν· ἑνδεκάτῃ κατενόει, κωματώδης δὲ ἦν, οὖρα πολλὰ, λεπτὰ καὶ μέλανα, ἄγρυπνος. εἶτ’ ἐφεξῆς ταῦτά φησι· ταύτῃ τὰ τῶν οὔρων διὰ τέλεος ἦν μέλανα καὶ λεπτὰ καὶ ὑδατώδεα, καὶ κῶμα παρείπετο, ἀπόσιτος, ἄγρυπνος, ἄθυμος.
